title: Is he mad? (Mark 3:20–30)
hookLine: his family think he's lost his mind; scribes say he's possessed
tomorrow: who are my mother and brothers?
last: APOSTLE — FIRST, TO BE WITH HIM.

lines: HIS OWN PEOPLE COME FOR HIM.
cards: Jesus comes into a house, and the crowd packs in so tight that, in the old King James words, they could not so much as eat bread. Word travels.
His own people hear what's going on, and they set out to bring him home by force. Mark doesn't soften what they were saying about him.
And while they're on the road, visitors arrive from Jerusalem: scribes, with a darker explanation of their own.

teach.b: In the King James Bible, they went to lay hold on him, "for they said, He is beside himself." Out of his mind. The Greek word pictures someone standing outside himself.
It's a startling thing for a gospel to include: the people who knew Jesus longest thought he'd lost it.
Then the scribes from Jerusalem go further. He has Beelzebul, they say, and he drives out demons by the prince of demons. Jesus doesn't shout.
He calls them over and tells them parables. How can Satan cast out Satan?
"And if a house be divided against itself, that house cannot stand." If the powers of evil were fighting themselves, they'd be finished already.

Then a picture: nobody can rob a strong man's house unless he ties up the strong man first. Christian tradition reads that as Jesus describing what he's doing: tying up evil and taking back what it stole.
Then a hard saying about the one sin that won't be forgiven, speaking against the Holy Spirit, and Mark explains it right away: they said he had an unclean spirit.

One common Christian reading takes it as calling God's good work evil, so stubbornly that a person won't turn back, and some pastors tell worried people that fearing you've done it is a sign you haven't.
In 1858 Abraham Lincoln borrowed it for a speech about a nation half slave and half free: a house divided against itself cannot stand.
Mark's story is also a sandwich: family sets out, scribes accuse, and tomorrow the family arrives.

how: Christian teaching commonly reads the strong-man picture as Jesus overcoming evil, and some Christians turn to this passage when their own family doesn't understand their faith.

s: the gospel hides that his family doubted him
Mark says it outright: his own people went to lay hold on him, saying he is beside himself.

Lincoln borrowed it in 1858 from Jesus's words in the gospels.

games.q: you're Jesus. important visitors say, in front of the crowd, that you work by the power of the devil. what do you do?
o: call them over and answer with parables.
ask the crowd to throw them out.
games.why: he calls them to him and answers in parables: how can Satan cast out Satan? a house divided cannot stand.

practice: Remember a time someone close got you wrong, someone who should have known better, and notice what comes back with it: the sting, maybe, or the wish to explain.
You don't have to win that argument in the next two minutes; you can let it be unfinished. If you pray, bring it to God as it is; if not, let it sit beside you without fighting it.

wordCard.voice: Beelzebul, the prince of demons the scribes accused Jesus of serving, answered with a question: how can Satan cast out Satan?

orig.note: Greek: he stood outside himself, he's out of his mind. The King James renders it, he is beside himself.

carryVoice: Your line: a house divided can't stand. Even his own people weren't sure of him. Day one hundred sixty-nine, in the books.
